home.guide_p1: Start from how much privacy you need and how comfortable you are with wallets. A decentralised exchange gives the most control and anonymity; an exchange with a no-KYC tier is easier and has deeper liquidity.
home.guide_p2: Look at trading fees, spreads and network fees together rather than the headline fee. Check that the coins and networks you need are supported, and that the platform has a clear history and answers when something goes wrong.
home.guide_p3: Make a small test deposit, trade and withdrawal before committing larger amounts. Spread counterparty risk across platforms and keep long-term holdings in self-custody.
home.guide_p4: Use a hardware or well-audited software wallet, check URLs and contract addresses, grant wallet permissions only when needed and avoid large custodial balances. No-KYC does not remove your legal or tax obligations, and it reduces your recourse if something goes wrong.
home.ad_p: Your tile carries a Sponsored label, reaches people who already avoid KYC, and leaves the directory order untouched. We review every advertiser first.
faq: Know Your Customer is the identity check regulated services run before letting you trade: ID card or passport, proof of address, sometimes a selfie. It exists for anti-money-laundering rules, and it concentrates sensitive data that can leak in a breach.

It depends on where you live. Using a platform that does not ask for ID is legal in most countries, but tax and reporting rules still apply to you. Decentralised protocols face less direct oversight; you stay responsible for following your local law.
What do None, Light and Tiered mean?
None: no ID and no account details. Light: no ID under a stated limit, or only an email or phone number. Tiered: ID is required above a threshold, written on each listing.
Which type of platform is best for beginners?

Start with an exchange that has a no-KYC tier: it works like the apps you know. A decentralised exchange gives the most privacy and control, but you need to be comfortable with a wallet and network fees.

Exchanges have tighter spreads and fast internal transfers. Decentralised exchanges show lower protocol fees but add network costs. Instant swaps build their margin into the quote, and ATMs add a cash-handling markup.

We build each listing from the platform's own terms and help pages, then re-check it over time. A paid test, when we run one, is dated on the listing. If a service removes no-KYC access or makes ID mandatory for its core features, we re-tag or remove it.

Some "Visit" buttons are affiliate links, marked on each platform page. We label every sponsored placement. Neither changes the order of the directory, which is sorted by the identity each platform asks for.
A listing is out of date. How do I report it?
Use the "Report a change" link on the platform’s page, or the one in the footer. We check every report before we update a listing.

tools.name: Tools
hub_intro: Wallets, VPNs, Tor and the other tools people use next to a no-KYC platform.
Each entry quotes what the maker says on its own site. A sponsor never buys a place on these pages.
tools.sort: Order: what the tool asks of you (nothing, an account, ID), then open code before closed code, then A to Z. Affiliate links and sponsors never change it.

vpn.name: VPN
intro: A VPN hides your IP address from the platform you use and your traffic from your internet provider. You now trust the VPN company instead.
Check how you pay and what the company says it logs.

tor.name: Tor and networks
intro: These networks pass your traffic through other computers before it reaches its destination. They run slower than a VPN.

dns.name: Encrypted DNS
intro: DNS turns a site name into an address. Encrypted DNS stops your internet provider from reading those requests. The resolver you pick reads them instead.

leak-tests.name: Leak tests
intro: Open one of these pages after you connect a VPN or Tor. It shows the IP address and DNS server the web sees.
Several of these sites belong to VPN companies.

routers.name: Routers
intro: Router software lets you set VPN and DNS rules for your whole home network.

wallets.name: Bitcoin wallets
intro: In a self-custody wallet you hold the keys, so no platform can ask you for ID to move your coins.
Buying inside a wallet usually goes through a third party that may ask for ID.

hardware-wallets.name: Hardware wallets
intro: A hardware wallet keeps your keys on a separate device.
Each entry shows whether the maker says its code is open.

monero-wallets.name: Monero wallets
intro: Wallets for Monero (XMR) on desktop and phone.
Each entry shows its latest release when the code is on GitHub.

privacy-coins.name: Privacy coins
intro: Coins built to hide amounts, senders or recipients.
Each entry quotes the project's own description.

private-payments.name: Private payments
intro: Ways to pay online without giving a merchant your card or phone number.
Some of them ask for ID. The entry says so.

desktop-os.name: Desktop systems
intro: Your operating system sees everything you do. These range from ordinary Linux distributions to systems built to leave no trace.
Several start from a USB stick or inside a virtual machine, so you can try them without wiping your computer.

mobile-os.name: Phone systems
intro: Each system below replaces the Android that ships on your phone. Check the device list first: each one runs on a short list of models.
Each entry says which devices it runs on.

email.name: E-mail
intro: An e-mail provider stores your messages and knows who you talk to. These providers say how they encrypt, where they sit and what they ask at sign-up.
Check what the provider asks at sign-up and how you can pay.

email-aliases.name: E-mail aliases
intro: An alias forwards mail to your real inbox, so a site never sees your real address. You turn an alias off as soon as it gets spam.

coinjoin.name: CoinJoin
intro: A CoinJoin is a Bitcoin transaction that several people build together to improve the privacy of their payments.
Some services have stopped: zkSNACKs closed its Wasabi coordinator on 1 June 2024, and the JoinMarket repository was archived in April 2026.

hardening.name: Privacy hardening
intro: Hardening means closing the gaps in the tools you already use: your browser, passwords, messages and files.
Start with what you use every day. Each entry says whether its code is open and what it asks of you.
